title: Bulk-Boundary Correspondence in Semi-Infinite Chains from Sublattice Zeros
authors: Ilya Iakoub, Nicolas Levasseur, Kylian Lionnet, Richard MacKenzie
abstract: We provide an alternative derivation of the bulk-boundary correspondence for semi-infinite chains. To describe edge states, we analytically continue the usual Bloch Hamiltonian to complex wave vectors $k$. To start, we note that the zeros of a Bloch wavefunction are related to edge states, at least in systems with nearest-neighbour hoppings. We show that an analytically continued Bloch Hamiltonian with chiral symmetry has exceptional points, where two different states coalesce. These special points are related to the adiabatic protection of edge states. We derive a winding number that counts the number of topological edge states protected by chiral symmetry.
summary: The paper derives a robust method to calculate the number of topologically protected edge states in semi-infinite chains by analyzing the zeros of analytically continued Bloch wavefunctions. It introduces and utilizes a winding number invariant that proves independent of arbitrary choices like unit cell definition, offering a superior tool for characterizing topological phases compared to traditional invariants.
main_problem: To provide an alternative, robust derivation of the bulk-boundary correspondence for topological edge states in semi-infinite chains.
main_result:
The number of topologically protected edge states is correctly counted by a winding number ($
u_B$) derived from analytically continued Bloch wavefunctions, which remains invariant even when changing the unit cell choice.
method: The analysis employs complex variable techniques, specifically analytic continuation of the Bloch Hamiltonian to $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and applying the Argument Principle (winding number calculation) on a specific contour in the complex plane.
model_or_system: The study analyzes semi-infinite chains, generalizing models like SSH chains, using an infinite chain Hamiltonian whose properties are analyzed via its continuation to complex wave vectors $z$. The system is characterized by hoppings and symmetries like chiral symmetry.
key_observables:
Winding numbers ($
u^{(m)}_b$, $
u_A$, $
u_B$), the number of edge states, and exceptional points (where two Bloch states coalesce).
important_parameters: The complex variable $z$ used for analytic continuation; parameters defining hopping strengths ($t_1, t_2, t_3$) and magnetic field ($B$).
main_assumptions: It is assumed that edge states can be derived from a single analytically continued Bloch state, and the winding number calculation assumes analyticity on the integration domain.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the complex plane domain $D = \{0 < |z| \leq 1\}$ used for contour integrals, showing zero trajectories during adiabatic evolution and phase diagrams related to exceptional points.
paper_structure:
The paper progresses by first establishing the analytic continuation method, then deriving a winding number invariant ($
u^{(m)}_b$) from boundary conditions, and finally comparing this result against other invariants (like the Zak phase) to prove its robustness across different unit cell choices.
why_interesting: This work provides powerful mathematical machinery—using complex analysis tools like winding numbers derived from analytically continued Hamiltonians—to rigorously count topological edge states in condensed matter systems, which is highly relevant for understanding boundary physics in quantum materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: The domain D and its boundary ∂D in the complex z plane. D consists of allowed values of z for a semi-infinite chain with boundary on the left. (Were the boundary on the right, the complimentary region (|z| > 1) would be allowed.) The appearance of states in each region are sketched.

FIG. 2: A possible trajectory, in complex z space, of a simple zero of α(m) b (z) during an adiabatic evolution. The large dot represents the point where |z0(t)| = 1, at which the non-analytically continued Bloch Hamiltonian has a state with a sublattice zero. In other words, at this point, the edge state becomes a bulk state: it crosses the band. In the scenario shown above, the edge state would disappear from the semi-infinite chain after crossing the |z| = 1 circle.
FIG. 3: An extension of the SSH model. Full black lines represent the hopping t1, dashed lines the hopping t2 and dotted lines represent the hopping t3.

FIG. 4: (Color online) Phase diagram describing the number of exceptional states with B = 0. e.p. in the legend stands for exceptional point. The x axis, we retrieve the usual results of the SSH model.
